col0: The Jersey Competition and Regulatory Authority (JCRA) currently only has the power to revoke a licence. Economic Development Minister Senator Alan Maclean said this was a "severe and often unrealistic measure". The proposal would enable JCRA to fine a telecom company up to 10% of their turnover. The fine would be based on the duration of the infraction, up to a maximum of three years. John Curran, chief executive of both the Jersey and Guernsey regulatory bodies, said the change would bring Jersey in line with most of the world, including Guernsey. "In Jersey, all you've got is two options, one is take the licence away from a company and the other is to send a letter to the company saying not to do it again," he said. The amendment to the telecommunication law would also include the ability for companies to appeal any fine or the amount of a fine. If approved, the consultation process the JCRA has to go through when issuing a new licence will also be simplified. The change is due to be debated on 6 December by the newly-elected States members.

col0: Beamish Museum in County Durham had 747,651 visitors last year, up 11% on the previous year. This is the first time it has seen more than 700,000 visitors in the 46 years it has been open, it said. Director Richard Evans said the income generated helped "not just Beamish but the whole region". "More than half of our visitors are tourists and nearly all of them stay overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and guest houses, as well as visiting the other cultural and heritage gems we have in this fantastic region," he said. There were 91,000 visitors in December, an increase of 38% on the same month the previous year, the museum said. Numbers have more than doubled since 2008, it said. Last year it was awarded £10.9m by the Heritage Lottery Fund to establish a 1950s-style town, a Georgian coaching inn and an upland farm that has been moved stone by stone from Weardale. The town will have a working cinema, shops, homes and bowling green. The former home of artist Norman Cornish will be replicated and a centre for older people will be housed in aged miners' homes. This the second fuel surcharge reduction for BA. It first cut the charge in October.

glass like stars strewn across tarmac,  
the sky holding its breath in the hush after impact.  
Rain began to fall, soft as regret,  
kissing chrome and crumpled steel.  

Paramedics moved like shadows through twilight,  
their voices low hymns against chaos.  
Somewhere, a phone rang unanswered;  
somewhere, a kettle boiled for tea that would go cold.  

He dreamed of open roads and summer winds,  
but woke to antiseptic light and silence.  
The world kept turning—buses rolled,  
children laughed, lovers kissed—  
while he lay still, stitched between life and maybe.  

Now every heartbeat echoes a question:  
*What if he’d left just one minute later?*

Just a day earlier, he had set a new national mark of 24.15—and now, he has pushed it even further. The crowd erupted as he touched the wall, clearly stunned by his back-to-back breakthroughs.

Ryan, whose mother is from Cork, has quickly become a fan favorite since declaring for Ireland. “It means everything,” he said post-race, still catching his breath. “I’ve felt so welcomed here, and I wanted to make the Irish people proud.” With the Olympics on the horizon, his rapid rise has sparked serious medal hopes. If he keeps this momentum, don’t be surprised to see him standing atop the podium—not just for Ireland, but on the world stage. One thing’s for sure

Rain-slicked tarmac, a sudden hush—  
where laughter once echoed through market-day thrush.  
His hands, still warm from morning’s last brew,  
now stilled beneath skies of mourning hue.  

The hedgerows weep with dew unspent,  
as neighbors whisper what the news lament.  
A son’s voice cracks on the phone’s thin line,  
a wife clutches silence, hollow as pine.  

That stretch of road—once just miles to cross—  
now bears the weight of unbearable loss.  
No engine hums where his car lay still,  
only wind through yew trees, soft and shrill.  

In chapel light and quiet street,  
Mold holds its breath in grief complete.  
Robert, gone—not just a name, but grace—

not just steel and concrete rising,

Nestled on the edge of the historic Borders town, the site hums with promise—cranes tracing arcs against summer skies, diggers carving foundations into red earth once trodden by monks and market traders. Designed to house both a modern primary school and a state-of-the-art care home, the campus fosters daily interaction between children and elders, weaving empathy into everyday life. Local stone and timber echo Jedburgh’s architectural heritage, while expansive windows invite light and connection. As saplings are planted alongside steel beams, the project embodies renewal—not just of infrastructure, but of relationships. Residents watch with quiet pride; this isn’t merely construction, but the careful laying of social bedrock for decades to come.

col0: Brighton and Hove City Council decided the attraction was "detrimental" to the nearby historic buildings and so would not stay open beyond May 2016. The owners of the wheel, which opened in 2011, said they will appeal. Brighton Wheel staff have been "guaranteed" an interview from the owners of a new attraction - the i360 viewing tower - which is being built. The firm had previously said it had wanted the wheel to close before the tower opens. Eleanor Harris, chief executive of the i360, said: "We will guarantee to interview all the Brighton Wheel staff when it closes next year." The city council said it will not renew the lease for the site where the wheel is based.

col0: The bridge, which crosses the River Thames, opened in September and allows cyclists and pedestrians from Caversham to access Reading Station and the town centre. Designed with sustainability and accessibility in mind, the new structure features wide walkways, dedicated cycle lanes, and energy-efficient lighting. Its construction marks a significant step in Reading’s efforts to reduce traffic congestion and promote greener modes of transport. Local authorities hope the bridge will encourage more residents to walk or cycle into town, thereby cutting carbon emissions and improving public health. Since its opening, usage has steadily increased, with many commuters praising the shorter, safer route it provides. The bridge also enhances connectivity between key residential and commercial areas, fostering stronger community links. Funded through a combination of local council investment and government grants, the project exemplifies how strategic infrastructure can support both environmental goals and urban development. Future plans include landscaping along the approach paths to further improve the user experience.

col0: The ex-MP for Chichester was one of nine new Tory peers announced by Theresa May last week. But questions were raised over whether this was an appropriate use of prime ministerial patronage, given his recent controversies. Critics pointed to his involvement in the 2019 expenses scandal, which contributed to his decision not to seek re-election. While appointments to the House of Lords are often used to reward political service, opposition figures argued that elevating individuals with contentious records undermines public trust in democratic institutions. A government spokesperson defended the nomination, citing the former MP’s long-standing contributions to local and national policy, particularly on rural affairs and defence. Nonetheless, transparency advocates called for clearer criteria governing peerages, urging reforms to the honours system to ensure greater accountability. The appointment adds to ongoing debates about the composition and legitimacy of the unelected upper chamber, as pressure mounts for broader constitutional review.
